title: Short Stuff: Johnny Appleseed
summary: Short Stuff episode on Johnny Appleseed, the real frontier nurseryman John Chapman. The hosts explain that the folk-tale image is largely accurate but he was a shrewd businessman rather than a carefree hippie. They cover apples originating in Kazakhstan, grafting versus planting from seed, and "spitters" (sour seed-grown apples, as described in a Smithsonian article). They discuss his Swedenborgian beliefs against grafting, the Ohio Company land requirement to plant fifty apple trees and twenty peach trees in three years, his nurseries, his role as a liaison with Native Americans, and the importance of hard cider on the frontier. The episode ends with prohibition-era destruction of apple trees and a surviving tree in Nova, Ohio said to be about 175 years old.

segments.title: Opening banter and Johnny Appleseed myth vs. reality
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode and say Johnny Appleseed was a real man, John Chapman, whose folk-tale image is mostly accurate. They argue he was a shrewd businessman, not a carefree flower child, and describe his honest, non-confrontational business dealings.

segments.title: Apple origins, grafting, and sour seed-grown apples
segments.summary: Apples are said to originate in Kazakhstan and became popular in Rome. Grafting is explained as the reliable way to reproduce desirable apple varieties, while seed-grown apples, called spitters, were very sour, as noted in a Smithsonian article and by Henry David Thoreau.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a break before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Swedenborgian beliefs and planting from seed
segments.summary: The hosts say Johnny Appleseed planted from seed rather than grafting because he belonged to the Swedenborgian church, which held that plants could feel and that grafting was therefore cruel.

segments.title: Ohio Company land requirement and nursery business
segments.summary: Chapman, from Ohio and born in Massachusetts, got land terms from the Ohio Company: a hundred acres if he planted fifty apple trees and twenty peach trees within three years. He saw a business opportunity in getting ahead of settlers, planting orchards, and selling land and nursery trees, doing this for decades along the moving frontier.

segments.title: Liaison with Native Americans and hard cider on the frontier
segments.summary: Chapman learned tribal languages, became a liaison and advocate for both settlers and Native Americans. Seed-grown apples were too sour to eat but made good hard cider, which was a staple of frontier life. Michael Pollan is cited on apples being used mostly for cider until Prohibition.

segments.title: Prohibition, Nova Ohio tree, and sign-off
segments.summary: Federal agents during Prohibition chopped down apple trees, and a 175-year-old tree on a farm in Nova, Ohio is said to possibly be the last tree Chapman planted. The hosts close with a mailing address.
